lead: A petrol engine needs a spark across a plug gap at the end of compression, at roughly 10–20 kV. The battery-coil ignition system makes that spark from a 12 V battery. Current flows in a low-voltage primary winding; a contact breaker opens the circuit; the collapsing magnetic field induces a high voltage in a secondary winding. A distributor sends this pulse to the correct cylinder. The same mechanism advances or retards the spark as speed and load change. It is also called the Kettering system or contact-point ignition, and it was the standard car ignition for decades.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for the battery, the ignition switch and high-voltage wiring, and the idea that a changing current makes a changing magnetic field.

blocks.text: An ignition system has four jobs. It must generate a voltage high enough to jump the plug gap: about 10–20 kV normally, more under heavy compression. It must send that pulse to the cylinder ready to fire. It must fire at the correct crank angle, a little before top dead centre (TDC), because the flame takes time to build pressure. It must vary that angle with speed and load: more speed needs more advance, heavy load needs less.

The arrangement that does all four with one coil is the battery-and-coil system, also called the Kettering system or contact-point ignition. A 12 V battery, an ignition switch and a ballast resistor feed the primary winding. The ballast resistor limits primary current; many circuits bypass it during cranking. A cam-driven contact breaker opens the primary circuit. A secondary winding sits on the same core. A distributor with a rotor and cap routes the secondary pulse to each plug in the firing order. The coil stores energy, the points time the pulse, and the distributor sends it out.

sections.h3: How the collapse makes high voltage

blocks.text: When the points close, current builds in the primary winding. This winding has a few hundred turns of thick wire, so its resistance is low and the current can reach several amperes. The current sets up a magnetic field in the iron core.
At the firing point, a cam lobe opens the points. Primary current falls to zero and the magnetic field collapses. A changing flux Φ through a winding induces an emf in every turn:

blocks.where: e is induced emf in volts (V); N is turns; Φ is magnetic flux in webers (Wb); t is time in seconds (s). The minus sign is Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change.

blocks.text: The same core links primary and secondary, so the changing flux induces an emf in both. This is mutual induction. The secondary has many thousands of turns of fine wire. Its emf is roughly e₂ = (N₂/N₁) × e₁ when both windings link the same flux. The speed of the collapse matters more than the turns ratio alone: a fast fall gives a large dΦ/dt. The secondary pulse goes through the distributor cap and rotor to one plug lead, then across that plug gap.

sections.h3: Dwell angle, dwell time and the capacitor

blocks.text: Dwell is the time the points stay closed. The coil needs enough dwell to build current; too little gives a weak spark, too much heats the coil. Dwell angle is the angle the distributor cam turns while the points are closed. Data books may quote it in distributor degrees or crank degrees. On a four-stroke engine the cam turns at half engine speed, so one distributor degree is two crank degrees.
Dwell time is the same interval in seconds:

blocks.where: θ_dwell is dwell angle in cam degrees; f_cam is cam revolutions per second.

blocks.text: For a multi-cylinder engine use the angle between sparks: dwell angle in crank degrees = dwell fraction × θ_spark.

A capacitor of about 0.2–0.3 μF sits across the points. When the points start to open, the primary current would jump the gap as an arc. The arc burns the points and keeps current flowing, so the field collapses slowly. The capacitor gives the current a short path and absorbs the energy. The primary circuit then oscillates and the current falls quickly, giving a high dΦ/dt and a high secondary voltage. The capacitor also stops arcing, so the points last.

The spark must occur earlier as speed rises: flame speed is roughly fixed while the piston moves faster. It must occur earlier at light load, because a lean mixture burns slowly. At heavy load, a rich mixture burns faster and too much advance can cause knock.

Centrifugal advance uses two weights on a plate driven by the distributor shaft. As speed rises, the weights swing outward and turn the cam relative to the shaft, so the points open earlier. Vacuum advance uses a diaphragm linked to the inlet manifold. Light load means high vacuum; the diaphragm pulls the breaker plate round and adds advance. Heavy load means low vacuum, and a spring removes the advance.

The result is an advance curve: spark advance in crank degrees before TDC against engine speed, with a vacuum correction for load. Base timing is set at idle with the vacuum pipe disconnected. The engine ECU in Chapter 2.3 replaces weights and diaphragms with a lookup table, but the two needs remain.

examples.question: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. The contact breaker dwell is 60% of the spark interval. Find the spark frequency, the spark interval, the dwell angle in crank degrees and the dwell time.
steps: A four-stroke cycle is 720° of crank. Four cylinders fire once each per cycle, so one spark every 720/4 = 180° of crank, i.e. two sparks per revolution.
Dwell angle = 0.60 × 180° = 108° of crank. On the distributor cam this is 108/2 = 54°.
examples.answer: Spark frequency = 100 sparks/s; spark interval = 10 ms; dwell angle = 108° of crank (54° of distributor); dwell time = 6 ms.
examples.check:
rpm = 3000
rev_per_s = rpm / 60
sparks_per_rev = 4 / 2
spark_freq = rev_per_s * sparks_per_rev
spark_interval_ms = 1000 / spark_freq
spark_angle = 720 / 4
dwell_fraction = 0.60
dwell_angle = dwell_fraction * spark_angle
dwell_time_ms = dwell_fraction * spark_interval_ms
print(spark_freq)
print(spark_interval_ms)
print(dwell_angle)
print(dwell_time_ms)

traps: Using rpm/60 as the spark frequency and forgetting the ×2 for a four-stroke four-cylinder engine.
Taking 60% of 360° instead of 60% of the angle between two sparks (180° of crank here).
Thinking the coil steps up a steady 12 V like a transformer. It needs the primary current to change, and the fast collapse makes the high voltage.
Saying the capacitor increases the spark energy directly. It suppresses arcing at the points, speeds the collapse and protects the points.
Confusing spark advance with firing order or with camshaft timing: advance means firing earlier before TDC.

quiz.q: State the four jobs of an ignition system.
quiz.a: Generate a high voltage to break the plug gap; distribute it to the correct cylinder; fire at the correct crank angle; vary timing with speed and load.

quiz.q: Define dwell angle and dwell time.
quiz.a: Dwell angle is the cam angle during which the points stay closed. Dwell time is the same closed interval in seconds.

quiz.q: Why does the secondary high voltage appear when the points open, not while they are closed?
quiz.a: While closed, primary current is steady, so flux is steady and dΦ/dt is zero. Opening the points collapses the flux quickly, and the changing flux induces a large emf in the secondary by mutual induction.

quiz.q: Why is a capacitor connected across the contact breaker points?
quiz.a: It gives the primary current a short path as the points open, so arcing is suppressed. The current falls quickly, giving a fast flux collapse and a high secondary voltage. It also reduces burning of the points.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 2400 rpm with dwell equal to 55% of the spark interval. Find the spark frequency, spark interval, dwell angle in crank degrees and dwell time.
quiz.a: 2400 rpm = 40 rev/s. Six cylinders give 3 sparks per revolution, so f = 120 sparks/s. T = 1/120 = 8.33 ms. Spark angle = 720/6 = 120° of crank. Dwell angle = 0.55 × 120° = 66° of crank. Dwell time = 0.55 × 8.33 ms = 4.58 ms.

quiz.q: At very high speed the dwell angle is fixed. Explain what happens to dwell time and to the spark.
quiz.a: Dwell time falls as speed rises because the same angle passes in less time. Primary current may not reach its full value, so the stored magnetic energy and secondary voltage fall. Electronic ignition controls dwell time or current instead of only angle.

quiz.q: Why does vacuum advance add spark advance at light load, and why is the vacuum pipe disconnected when setting base timing?
quiz.a: Light load gives high manifold vacuum; the diaphragm moves the breaker plate and advances the spark for a slow-burning lean mixture. Disconnecting the pipe removes this advance so the idle base timing can be set without vacuum correction.

quiz.q: Base timing is 8° BTDC. Centrifugal advance adds 20° at 3000 rpm and vacuum advance adds 6° at light load. Find the total advance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars moved from contact points to electronic switching, then to coil-on-plug systems where each plug has its own coil; see Chapter 2.4. Research ignition now includes ion-sensing, where the spark plug also measures combustion, and capacitive discharge ignition for very fast voltage rise. Search terms: Kettering ignition, dwell control, ionization current sensing, capacitive discharge ignition.
